entities.summary:
Works and Days

Identity & Significance: Hesiod's didactic poem, created around 800 BCE, is one of the oldest surviving works of Greek literature. Written in dactylic hexameter, it instructs his brother Perses on agriculture and offers a glimpse into ancient Greek culture and values. As a key work of the Archaic period, Works and Days provides valuable insights into the lives of early Greeks and their understanding of the natural world.

What Happened: The poem describes Hesiod's experiences with his father Zeus, who is said to have stolen his cattle, and his subsequent journey to the underworld to reclaim them. Along the way, he encounters various figures from Greek mythology, including the three-headed dog Cerberus and the goddess Athena.

Legacy & Consequence: Works and Days had a significant impact on Western literature, influencing later works such as Virgil's Georgics and Dante's Divine Comedy. Its themes of agriculture, nature, and the human condition continue to resonate with readers today.

Did Hesiod's work 'bring light into our lives'?', as the ancient Greek poet himself described his art in the Works and Days?
